title: Your first real test, and why assertions matter

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 5 - TypeScript - Arrow functions, `async`, and reading `import`

By the end of this lesson you'll be comfortable writing an arrow function, know exactly
when to put `async` in front of one, be able to read `({ page }) => { ... }`, and be able to
read a single `import` line — everything today's Playwright code (and every test you'll ever
write in this course) needs from the language before you meet the Playwright API itself.

> **This lesson is TypeScript only.** No browsers, no Playwright. That starts in
> [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) — and this is the **first time in the whole course** you'll see
> arrow functions and `async`, so take it slowly; everything later builds on it.

> **Every run starts fresh.** Each time you press Run, your code starts from a clean slate. Nothing from a previous run is still in memory.

## What today needs

| # | Concept | Where it shows up in every Playwright test |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Arrow functions | The function passed to `test(...)` |
| 2 | `async` arrow functions | Almost every Playwright action needs `await`, so almost every test function is `async` |
| 3 | Destructuring in a parameter list | `async ({ page }) => {}` — how a test receives its tools |
| 4 | `import { x } from "package"` | The line at the top of every spec file |

## 1. Arrow functions

**What it is.** A function written inline, without the `function` keyword. `(parameters) =>
expression` — if the body is a single expression, it's returned automatically, no `return`
needed.

**Why it exists.** It's shorter to write and to read than `function(...) {...}` for the small,
one-off functions you pass *into* something else — which is exactly what a test is: a
function you hand to `test(...)`.

**Syntax**

```ts
const name = (param1, param2) => expression;          // implicit return
const name = (param1, param2) => { /* ...; return x; */ };  // block body, explicit return
```

Line by line:

| Line | What it does |
|---|---|
| `(n: number) => n * n` | Takes `n`, returns `n * n` — no braces, no `return` keyword, it's implied |
| `(name: string) => { ... }` | Braces switch it to a normal function body — now `return` is required |

**Expected result:** `25`, then `hello, Leela`.

**Challenge:** write a one-line arrow function `double` that returns `n * 2`, with no braces.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same two shapes, different logic: write a single-expression arrow that cubes a number, and a block-body arrow that builds a farewell message from a name.

blocks.text:
## 2. `async` arrow functions

**What it is.** The same arrow function, with `async` in front. An `async` function always
returns a Promise, and lets you use `await` inside its body to pause until another Promise
settles.

**Why it exists.** JavaScript doesn't block while something slow happens (a network request, a
browser action, a timer) — it moves on and comes back when the result is ready. `await` is how
you say "pause *this* function specifically until that result arrives", without freezing the
whole program. Every Playwright action (`click`, `fill`, `goto`, `waitFor`...) returns a
Promise, which is exactly why Playwright code is full of `await`, and why the function
containing it must be `async`.

**Syntax**

```ts
const name = async (param) => {
  const result = await somethingSlow(param);
  return result;
};
```

**Expected result:** a ~200ms pause, then `hello (after a pause), Katy`.

**The rule to remember:** if the body of your arrow function uses `await`, the function
*must* be declared `async` — leaving it off is a TypeScript compile error, not a silent bug.
For Playwright code, the body almost always awaits something, so the function is almost
always `async`.

**Challenge:** remove `async`/`await` from `slowGreet` and read the compiler's complaint
before putting them back.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same pattern, a different message: write your own wait-based async function that pauses, then returns a goodbye message instead of a greeting.

blocks.text:
## 3. Destructuring in the parameter list

**What it is.** Instead of naming the whole object a function receives, you can pull specific
fields straight out of it in the parameter list itself: `({ field1, field2 }) => {}`.

**Why it exists.** Playwright hands your test function an object full of tools ("fixtures") —
`page`, `browser`, `browserName`, and more. Destructuring lets you ask for only the one or two
you actually need, by name, instead of writing `tools.page` everywhere.

**Syntax**

```ts
const name = ({ field }: { field: Type }) => { /* use field directly */ };
```

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same destructured-parameter shape, different fields: write a one-line arrow that takes `{ city, country }` and returns a formatted "city, country" string.

blocks.text:
## 4. Reading `import { x } from "package"`

**What it is.** A line that pulls named values out of another file or package. `{ test }`
means "give me specifically the thing named `test` that this package exports" — not the whole
package, just that one piece (a **named import**).

You don't need a full lecture on JavaScript modules to read one import line — just enough to
recognize the shape:

```ts
import { test } from "@playwright/test";
```

This says: "from the `@playwright/test` package, give me the thing it exports named `test`."
That's the `test(...)` function every spec file calls.

> One thing to flag: this exact line only works inside a real `.spec.ts` file run by
> `npx playwright test` — not in an explore-mode lesson cell like this one. You've already
> seen why in the "Mode" banners on Days 2–4: `@playwright/test` only exists inside the real
> test-runner process. So this line is shown here to read, not to run.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same shape again, applied to Playwright: write a one-line arrow that takes `{ page, isMobile }` and returns a string describing them, the way `showFixtures` did for `page`/`browserName`.

blocks.text:
## Recap

| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| `(x) => expr` | Inline function; no braces means the value is returned automatically |
| `async (x) => { await ... }` | Required whenever the body awaits something — which, for Playwright, is always |
| `({ page }) => {}` | Pulls just the `page` fixture out of everything Playwright offers — the shape of every test |
| `import { test } from "@playwright/test"` | Named import — one specific export, from one specific package |

**Next:** [Fundamentals - Your first real test](/learn/w1/d5/p2)
`const square = (n: number) => n * n;` has no `return`. Why does it still return a value?

options: Arrow functions return their last statement automatically
A body with no braces is a single expression, and its value is returned implicitly
`return` is optional everywhere in TypeScript
checkpoint.explanation: No braces means the arrow is followed by one expression, and that expression's value is the return value. Add braces and you are back to a normal function body, where `return` is required — a difference that catches people the first time a block-bodied arrow silently returns `undefined`.

blocks.text: You write an arrow function whose body calls `await page.click(...)` but you leave off `async`. What happens?

options: It runs, but the click may not finish before the next line
A TypeScript compile error — `await` is only valid inside an `async` function
It runs and silently ignores the `await`
checkpoint.explanation: This one fails loudly at compile time rather than misbehaving at run time, which is the good case. Since practically every Playwright action returns a Promise, practically every test body awaits something — which is why practically every test function is `async`.

blocks.text: In `test("name", async ({ page }) => { ... })`, what is `({ page })` doing?

options: Declaring a parameter that happens to be called page
Destructuring just the `page` fixture out of the object of tools Playwright passes in
Creating a new page object for the test to use
checkpoint.explanation: Playwright hands the test one object containing every fixture it could offer — `page`, `browser`, `browserName` and more. Destructuring in the parameter list pulls out only the ones you name, so you write `page` rather than `tools.page` throughout. Nothing is being created here; it is being unpacked.

parts.title: Your first real test, and why assertions matter

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 5 - Fundamentals - Your first real test, and why assertions matter

By the end of this lesson you will have written and run a real Playwright test, and — this
is the important part — **watched a test pass when it should have failed**, because it never
checked anything. Then you'll fix it and watch it fail correctly.

Prerequisites are in [TypeScript](/learn/w1/d5/p1). If arrow functions or `async` felt shaky, go
back — everything below assumes you're comfortable reading `async ({ page }) => {}`.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Goals** | Watch a test pass with the wrong password because it checks nothing, then fix it and watch it fail correctly. |
| **Prerequisites** | [arrow functions, `async`, destructuring](/learn/w1/d5/p1) |
| **Environment** | in your own project. These need the Playwright test runner. |
| **Key takeaway** | a test that only acts and never asserts is a recording, not a test |
> **Follow this one in your own project.** These examples are run by the Playwright test runner, which the editor here does not provide. Copy them into your own checkout to run them.

## Example — log in, and watch it "pass" even though it shouldn't

**Objective:** write the login flow from Day 4 as a real test — but deliberately leave out any
assertion — and use a **wrong password**. Watch what the report says.

> ▶ **Run it yourself too:** `npx playwright test week1/generated/day5-assertions-gap.spec.ts`

**Expected result:** the first test reports as **passed**, and the second **fails** with a
real Playwright error (`expect(page).toHaveURL(expected) failed`). Overall: `1 failed`,
`1 passed`.

Read that first result again. Both tests typed the *exact same wrong password*. Login
genuinely did not succeed in either case — the banking app just silently stays on the login
page with no error message (verified: correct email + wrong password → no redirect, no
message at all). The first test still reports green, because **automation never finds a
defect — it only reports pass or fail against a check a human wrote** ([Day 1 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d1/p2)). No check was
written, so there was nothing to fail.

This is the single most important lesson of the week: a Playwright test that only performs
actions and never asserts is not testing anything. It's a recording.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same gap, Katy's credentials: write the two-test spec again, but log in as Katy with a wrong password instead of Leela.

blocks.text:
## Fixing it

The second test above already has the fix: a real assertion.

```ts
await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/, { timeout: 5000 });
```

`expect(page).toHaveURL(...)` is Playwright's **auto-retrying** assertion — it polls until the
URL matches or the timeout elapses, then fails loudly with a real error message (not a silent
"nothing happened") if it never does. That's the whole difference between the two tests
above: one performs actions, the other performs actions *and checks a consequence*.

An equally valid fix, using this app's real signed-in-user locator:

```ts
await expect(page.getByText("Leela")).toBeVisible();
```

Either one turns "did something happen" into "did the *right* thing happen".

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same gap, a different missing assertion: this time, the second test should check the page URL stays on the login page instead of checking for the dashboard redirect.

blocks.text:
## Best practices

- Every test needs at least one `expect()` that would actually fail if the feature broke.
- Prefer asserting the **consequence** (reached the dashboard, saw the user's name) over
  asserting that an action merely "didn't throw" — a `.click()` succeeding proves the button
  was clickable, not that login worked.
- Read a passing test with suspicion the first time you write it: what would make this go
  red? If the answer is "nothing", it isn't testing anything yet.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| A test with only actions, no `expect()` | Always green, regardless of whether the feature works | Add an assertion on the actual consequence |
| Asserting `.toBeVisible()` on something that's always in the DOM | Passes whether or not the real condition happened | Assert on something that genuinely changes (URL, a specific text) |
| Assuming a wrong-password login throws an error | It doesn't — this app just silently stays put | Assert the *positive* outcome (`toHaveURL(/dashboard/)`), not the absence of a crash |
Both tests type the same wrong password. Why does the first one report green?

options: The app accepted the wrong password, so the login really did succeed
It contains no `expect()`, so there was nothing that could fail
Playwright treats a failed login as a warning rather than an error
checkpoint.explanation: Login genuinely failed in both tests — verified: this app just stays on the login page, with no error message at all. The first test performed four actions, none of which threw, and reported success. "Automation never finds a defect" from [Day 1](/learn/w1/d1/p2) stops being an abstraction right here.

blocks.text: Which assertion actually proves the login worked?

options: `await expect(page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" })).toBeVisible()` before clicking
`await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/)` after clicking
Checking that `.click()` completed without throwing
checkpoint.explanation: Assert the **consequence**. A click completing proves the button was clickable, not that anything happened afterwards; asserting the login button is visible proves you are still looking at the login page. Only a successful login changes the URL or makes the user's name appear.

blocks.text: What question should you ask of a test you have just written and watched pass?

options: Does it run fast enough to keep in the suite?
What would make this go red? If the answer is "nothing", it is not testing anything yet.
Does it cover every element on the page?
checkpoint.explanation: A green test is only meaningful if some realistic breakage would turn it red. Reading your own passing test with suspicion is the habit this day exists to build. Apply it the moment you write the test, not after it has been green through six broken releases.

blocks.text:
- **A test with no `expect()` cannot fail for the right reason.** It is a recording of actions.
- Assert the consequence, such as the URL or the user's name. Do not settle for an action that merely did not throw.
- `expect(page).toHaveURL(...)` auto-retries until it matches or times out, then fails with a real message.
- This app gives no error on a wrong password: it just stays put. Silence is not success.
- Ask of every passing test: what would make this go red?

## What's next

[Implementation](/learn/w1/d5/p3) takes this exact login code and gives it a small amount of structure —
a first look at the shape you'll use for the rest of the course.

parts.title: The same login, with a little structure

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 5 - Implementation - The same login, with a little structure

By the end of this lesson you will have seen the [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) lesson's exact login steps reorganized into a
small class — a first, gentle look at the shape you'll build on for the rest of the course.

> **The same calls, a new shape.** `getByPlaceholder`, `getByRole`, `fill` and `click` all
> come from [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2); the structure around them is what is new. The
> class is written **inline in the spec file below**, as a shape to recognise rather than a
> file the repo ships.

> This previews something week5 names and covers in full depth as the **Page Object Model** —
> today, just notice the shape; you don't need the name yet.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | three repeated locators become a class built once, and one named `signIn` step |
| **Tools** | the same locators and actions from [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) |
| **Scope** | This structure is the Page Object Model. Week 5 names it and covers it in full. |
| **Key takeaway** | a page object never asserts |

## The problem with the Fundamentals lesson's version

Both tests in [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) repeat the same three lines — find the email box, find the password
box, find the login button — before doing anything different. In a real suite with dozens of
login-adjacent tests, that's dozens of copies of the same three locators. Redesign the login
form, and you're editing every single test.

## Same code, with structure around it

| In [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) you wrote | Here it becomes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `page.getByPlaceholder("Enter Email")` (typed fresh in every test) | `this.emailBox` (built once, in the constructor) | One place to update if the form changes |
| `await page.getByPlaceholder("Enter Email").fill(email)` then 2 more lines | `await loginPage.signIn(email, password)` | The *steps* to log in are named once, as one action |
| A test that both logs in and could check the result inline | The class contains **no `expect()`** — the test still decides what's true | Reusable by tests expecting success *and* tests expecting failure |

> ▶ **Run it yourself too:**
> `npx playwright test week1/generated/day5-login-page-shape.spec.ts`

**Expected result:** `2 passed` — one test proves the class works for a correct login, the
other proves it works (i.e. correctly stays put) for a wrong password. Same class, both
outcomes — because it doesn't decide what "correct" means; the tests do.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same class, Katy's login: reuse `LoginPage.signIn`, but prove it for Katy's credentials instead of Leela's.

blocks.text:
## Why it's shaped this way

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| Locators built once in the constructor, marked `readonly` | One place to change when the app is redesigned; `readonly` stops a method reassigning one by accident |
| A method named `signIn`, not `fillFormAndClick` | Reads like something a *user* does, not a list of DOM operations |
| **No `expect()` anywhere inside the class** | The class only knows how to act on the page — it has no opinion on what should be true. That's the test's job. |

## The one rule worth memorizing: no assertions in a page object

It's tempting to put the check inside `signIn` — you already have `page` right there. Resist
it. The moment a page object asserts something, it can only be reused by tests that want
*that exact* assertion — and you end up with `signIn`, `signInAndCheckDashboard`,
`signInAndCheckWrongPassword`, one method per outcome. The version above that asserts nothing
is reusable by every test in this lesson, and every test you'll write for the rest of the
course.

This is also one of the few design questions that comes up in interviews, so being able to
explain *why*, not just recite the rule, is worth more than the rule itself.
Why does `LoginPage` contain no `expect()` at all?

options: Because assertions are not allowed outside a `test()` body
So it can be reused by tests expecting success AND tests expecting failure — the test decides what should be true
Because the class runs before the test does
checkpoint.explanation: Put the check inside `signIn` and it only suits tests wanting that exact outcome. You then grow `signInAndCheckDashboard`, `signInAndCheckWrongPassword`, one method per outcome. The version that asserts nothing serves both tests in this very lesson — one expecting a dashboard, one expecting to stay put.

blocks.text: The locators are built once in the constructor and marked `readonly`. What does `readonly` buy?

options: It stops a method reassigning a locator by accident
It makes the locators resolve once and cache the element
It is required for TypeScript to infer the `Locator` type
checkpoint.explanation: It is a compile-time guarantee about the field, nothing more. A locator is a live reference that re-resolves on every use. `readonly` does not freeze what it points at; it only fixes which locator the field holds.

blocks.text:
- Three locators repeated across dozens of tests is dozens of edits when the form is redesigned. Build them once.
- Name a method for what a **user** does (`signIn`), not for the DOM operations inside it.
- **No assertions in a page object.** It knows how to act; the test decides what should be true.
- `readonly` guards the field, not the element — a locator still re-resolves every time it is used.
- You are looking at the Page Object Model. Week 5 gives it its name and its full treatment.

## What's next

[Practice](/learn/w1/d5/p4) — your turn, with no worked examples to lean on. This closes out
Week 1; Week 3 picks up from here with timeouts, hooks, and the real config file in depth.

parts.title: Practice: your first test, and the assertions gap

blocks.text:
# Week 1 - Day 5 - Practice - Your first test, and the assertions gap

Three problems, capping off the week. No solutions — you'll know you're right because the
report will tell you.

Write specs into `week1/generated/` and run them with `npx playwright test`, same as every
example this week.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Three problems that close the week: a test of your own, the assertions gap, and a small page object. The test report tells you whether each answer is correct. |
| **Scope** | These problems close Week 1, which covered why teams automate, setup, the CLI, Codegen, and the assertion that makes a test a test. |

## When you're done

You've now written a real test, watched it lie to you, fixed it, and given it a first bit of
structure. That's the whole arc of this week. Week 3 picks up from here — timeouts, hooks and
isolation, and the config file in real depth.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Write the login test from [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) again, from memory, for a **different**
demo user — Katy (`katy@gmail.com` / `Katy@12354`) or Jyosthna (`jyosthna@gmail.com` /
`Jyos@123`). Use a real `expect()` this time, from the start.

**Where.** `week1/generated/day5-practice-login.spec.ts`.

**How you'll know it worked.** `1 passed`, and the test would genuinely fail if you typed the
wrong password — try that once on purpose to confirm.

> **Hint** — `_shared/deno-helpers.ts` has all three users in `USERS`, in case you want to
> check the exact spelling rather than retyping from memory.

**What to build.** Recreate the [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) lesson's exact demonstration from scratch: one test that logs in
with a wrong password and asserts **nothing** (confirm it passes), then add a real
`expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/)` to the *same* test and re-run it (confirm it now
fails). Write one sentence on what changed in the report between the two runs.

**Where.** `week1/generated/day5-practice-gap.spec.ts`, edited and re-run once.

**How you'll know it worked.** You personally watched the exact same test go from
`1 passed` to `1 failed` by adding one line — not just read that it does.
problems.stub:
// Problem 2 — your code here. Run it once without the assertion, note the result,
// add the assertion, run it again, note the result.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** A tiny two-method page object: `signIn(email, password)` (like the [Implementation](/learn/w1/d5/p3) lesson's
`LoginPage`) plus a second method that reads and returns the signed-in user's name (using
`page.getByText(name)` — no `exact: true`, per `_shared/CONCEPTS.md`). Then write a test that
uses the class and asserts on its return value — **no locator should appear in the test file
itself**, only inside the class.

**Where.** `week1/generated/day5-practice-pageobject.spec.ts`.

**How you'll know it worked.** `1 passed`, and re-reading your test file, every `page.getBy...`
call lives inside the class, not the test.
